While Baghdad Was Burning, the ʿUlamāʾ Were Quarrelling over the Permissibility of Eating Crows and Owls!

— Times change, circumstances change, but our sense of priorities in intellectual discourse seems hardly to change!

For the past few days, whenever I open Facebook, various posts debating the permissibility of eating *jarda* (a form of betel-leaf preparation containing tobacco and other ingredients) have caught my attention. Arguments supporting and opposing the fatwa, counterarguments, and rebuttals—the discussion has become quite lively and, in its own way, entertaining!

Of course, I am not a mufti, nor am I qualified to issue fatwas on matters of ḥalāl and ḥarām. Nevertheless, like many others, this discussion has caught my attention.

It brings to mind a widely circulated historical anecdote.

According to popular accounts, when Hulagu Khan’s Mongol forces laid siege to Baghdad in 1258 CE and the fall of the city was imminent, some of the ʿulamāʾ were still engrossed in debating whether the meat of crows and owls was ḥalāl or ḥarām.

It is said that Hulagu Khan sent a spy to assess the situation in the city. Upon returning, the spy informed him that Baghdad’s rulers and ʿulamāʾ seemed more preoccupied with determining whether eating crow and owl meat was permissible than with the impending catastrophe facing their city.

According to the anecdote, upon hearing this report, Hulagu Khan ordered his troops to advance rapidly towards Baghdad.

Another similar popular anecdote relates that—

It is said that even as the city's defences were collapsing and Mongol siege engines were pounding its walls, some people remained occupied with fine points of jurisprudence concerning the precise length of the *miswāk*—how many inches or finger-widths it should be to conform to the Sunnah.

The historical authenticity of these stories is certainly open to question. Nevertheless, the underlying satire of these anecdotes is quite significant.

Discussions of detailed rulings on religious matters are undoubtedly necessary. But when a major crisis is unfolding all around us, should we not also possess the sense of priority to recognise which matters are more urgent and which discussions are truly demanded by the circumstances of the time?

Sometimes I cannot help feeling:

**Times change, circumstances change, but our sense of priorities in intellectual discourse seems hardly to change!**
